engine.title: The multibagger screen qualified nobody for four weeks
engine.body: Corrects what this entry said on 2026-08-27. It read ‘the scan is running on schedule’ and blamed the fixed list on cadence. The ledger says otherwise: the last multibagger row is 2026-08-01, while magic, magicmagic and ai_longterm — the same Saturday job, the same slot — all logged 2026-08-22. Twenty-six days, three Saturdays, nothing written.
engine.note: The screen is not broken. Run on 2026-08-27 it took 11 candidates and rejected 10 for R:R below 2.0 — CHENNPETRO 1.29, FLUOROCHEM 1.07, GLAXO 0.59, which needs a 63% win rate merely to break even. The defect was that a week qualifying nobody wrote nothing at all, so the page served the 1 August list as though it were current. The attempt is recorded either way now. The gate is NOT loosened: publishing a 0.59 R:R to keep the section busy is the exact trade this screen exists to refuse, and an empty week is a real result.

engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Strategy: Weak Squares
chess.body: A weak square is one that cannot be defended by a pawn. d5 is weak for Black if the c6 and e6 pawns are gone or never played. Plant a knight on a weak square — it becomes an 'outpost.' From d5, a knight controls 8 squares and cannot be chased. Outpost knight + weak squares = long-term advantage.

wisdom.title: The Compound Effect of Small Moments
wisdom.body: You don't build a relationship in big moments. You build it in 10,000 small ones. Morning hugs. Saying her name with warmth. Listening when she babbles even though you don't understand. These stack. In 15 years, she'll feel either deeply loved or quietly neglected. Both are built today.

book.author: Morgan Housel
book.lesson: In investing and in life, a small number of events account for the majority of outcomes. Venture capital funds know that 1 investment out of 50 will return the entire fund. Amazon's success is almost entirely explained by AWS — which started as an internal experiment. Housel's lesson: you can be wrong most of the time and still be enormously successful if you're right on the few things that matter most. This means long tail bets matter. Staying in the game long enough to hit the tails matters. Avoiding ruin so you can be there for the rare extraordinary outcomes matters most.
book.key_quote: You only need to be right a few times in your life, as long as you don't catastrophically lose the ability to keep playing.
book.action: Identify the two or three decisions in your career/portfolio that would be truly transformative. Optimise for those, not the daily noise.
crux: Doing well with money has little to do with intelligence and everything to do with behaviour.
No one is crazy. Every money decision makes sense given that person's specific history of experience.
Luck and risk are the shadow siblings of every outcome. Neither is measurable, both are decisive.
There is no reason to risk what you have for what you don't need.
Compounding is counterintuitive: $81.5bn of Buffett's $84.5bn arrived after his 65th birthday.
Getting money and keeping money are different skills. The second requires frugality and paranoia.
Tails drive everything. A minority of events account for the majority of outcomes.
The highest dividend money pays is control over your own time.
Wealth is what you don't see. Spending is evidence of spending, not of wealth.
Save without a specific goal. Savings buy optionality against a world you cannot forecast.
Room for error is the single most underrated force. Plan for the plan not going to plan.
Avoid extreme financial commitments — your future self's goals will not match your current ones.
Volatility is the fee for high returns, not a fine for a mistake. Fees you pay willingly; fines you avoid.
Define the game you are playing, and stop taking cues from people playing a different one.
learnings: A mediocre strategy held for 30 years beats a brilliant one abandoned in year 3.
Most financial mistakes are emotional, so most financial fixes must be behavioural.
Survival is the prerequisite for compounding. Everything else is secondary.
Your risk tolerance is not a number. It is what you actually do at a 40% drawdown.
examples: Ronald Read, a petrol-station attendant, left $8m by buying blue chips for decades. Richard Fuscone, Harvard MBA and Merrill executive, went bankrupt in 2008.
Bill Gates went to one of the only high schools on earth with a computer in 1968 — one in a million odds. His equally able friend Kent Evans died climbing.
Buffett's returns are good but not historically unique; his 80-year runway is. Start at 30 instead of 10 and the fortune largely disappears.
adapt: SIP ₹5–15K/month for the BMW fund. The consistency matters more than the monthly amount.
Keep 6 months of KL expenses liquid before scaling any trading capital. Room for error first.
Trading capital is separate from family capital. Never one pool.
The Dubai target is AED 30K/month, not 'as much as possible'. Define enough or the goalpost moves forever.

minimalism.title: The 90/90 Rule
minimalism.body: Have you used it in the last 90 days? Will you in the next 90? If both answers are no, it is storage, not ownership. You are paying rent on it in square feet and attention.
minimalism.action: Pick one drawer. Apply 90/90 to every item in it.
minimalism.label: Minimalism

etiquette.title: Phone Face Down, Or Away
etiquette.body: A visible phone halves the perceived quality of a conversation — measurably, in studies. Face down is the minimum. Out of sight is the standard.
etiquette.action: Phone in your bag, not on the table, for every conversation today.
etiquette.label: Etiquette

stillness.title: Memento Mori
stillness.body: You will die. Marcus Aurelius wrote it to himself daily while running an empire. Not morbid — clarifying. It sorts the urgent from the important in about four seconds.
stillness.action: Ask of one commitment: would this matter if I had a year left?
stillness.label: Stillness

model.title: Via Negativa
model.body: Improvement by removal. Subtracting a bad habit, a bad client, or a bad process is more reliable than adding a good one, and the effect is immediate.
model.action: Remove one thing today rather than adding an improvement.
model.label: Mental Model

arabic.use: Attached to any future plan. Culturally expected — its absence sounds presumptuous about the future.
arabic.label: Arabic

drill.title: Steelman The Other Side
drill.body: Argue the opposing position better than its advocates do. Until you can, you do not understand your own position — you just prefer it.
drill.action: Write the strongest case against a view you hold firmly.
drill.label: Drill

health.title: Consistency Beats Optimisation
health.body: The perfect protocol you follow 30% of the time loses to the adequate one you follow 90% of the time. Every fitness argument online is about the last 5% and ignores the first 95%.
health.action: Pick the minimum session you would do on your worst week. That is your floor.
health.label: Health

quote.name: Evan Spiegel
quote.quote: Because there are so many bad companies out there, it is actually quite easy to succeed.

lesson.lesson: Plant trees under whose shade you do not plan to sit.

case.title: Swiggy vs Zomato: The Profitability Race
case.story: Both companies burned billions. Zomato reached profitability first by cutting dark stores, focusing on Blinkit synergies, and raising average order value.
case.lesson: In competitive markets, the winner is often whoever cuts losses fastest and finds profitability before their competitor. Endurance beats speed.

fpna.title: Dubai FP&A Stack
fpna.body: AED 30K+ roles: CA/ACCA + Power BI + SAP or Oracle + IFRS 9/16. Targets: ADNOC, Emirates, MAF, DP World.

cfo.title: CFO Step 3: M&A Fundamentals
cfo.body: Basic M&A literacy: DCF valuation, EV/EBITDA multiples, due diligence process, SPA (Share Purchase Agreement), earn-out structures. You don't need to be an investment banker, but you need to read a deal memo and ask smart questions.

money_hack.title: ELSS Lock-in Trick
money_hack.body: ELSS 3-year lock-in: SIP each month → each instalment unlocks separately. Best 80C option.

dubai.title: Why applications stall at 60%
dubai.body: Most Gulf portals reject on missing fields, not on merit. Passport number, visa status, notice period, current and expected salary. Leave one blank and the application never reaches a human.
dubai.targets: Expected salary blank is read as 'unclear', which is worse than a high number.
dubai.action: Keep a text file with every field the portals ask for. Paste, do not retype.

desk.productivity: 90-min deep work sprints. No phone. Door closed. Results compound.

father.title: Sing the same song at the same moment
father.do: Attach one song to one transition — nappy change, bath, car seat.
father.why: Predictable audio cues reduce transition resistance because she knows what comes next. It is the cheapest behavioural tool available at this age.

father.title: Give her something to solve
father.do: Put a favourite toy just inside an open container so she has to reach in.
father.why: Means-end reasoning — using one action to achieve a separate goal — is developing now. Small solvable problems build it; unsolvable ones just frustrate.

life_wisdom.teaching: The endless wanting that survives every acquisition. Jain and Buddhist thought agree closely here — the object changes, the wanting does not.
life_wisdom.apply: Notice the next thing you tell yourself you will be satisfied after getting. Write it down. Check in six months whether the satisfaction arrived.

life_wisdom.teaching: The mind's tendency to spin a single perception into an elaborate narrative — one ambiguous email becoming a theory about your standing at work.
life_wisdom.apply: When you notice the story running, return to what actually happened, stated in one sentence with no interpretation. The gap is usually startling.

vocab.example: This is a systemic control weakness, not an isolated error.
vocab.note: Not 'systematic', which means methodical. The two get confused in audit reports constantly.

vocab.example: Shrinkage at that level is endemic to the format, not to the store.
vocab.note: Distinguishes a structural feature from a local failure — useful when defending a manager.

speaking.title: Vary sentence length
speaking.drill: Speak for 90 seconds deliberately alternating one short sentence and one longer one.
speaking.why: Monotone rhythm loses a room faster than monotone pitch. Your writing already does this — make speech match.

interview_tech.q: How do you build a rolling 13-week cash forecast?
interview_tech.a: Direct method, receipts and payments, not derived from P&L. Start with confirmed opening bank. Layer in: daily sales collections by tender type with settlement lag; supplier payment runs from the AP ageing; payroll on fixed dates; rent on quarter days; tax and VAT on statutory dates; capex from approved commitments. Roll it weekly and track forecast versus actual variance by line — the discipline is in explaining last week's miss, which is what makes week 13 credible.

interview_tech.q: Your forecast missed by 12%. The CEO asks why in the board meeting.
interview_tech.a: Answer in this order: the number, the driver, the fix, the revised view. 'We missed by AED 14M. Eleven of that is two categories where sell-through ran 20 points below plan; three is timing on a store opening that slipped a quarter. The buying calendar for those categories is now locked four weeks later so we commit on actual trend. Revised full-year is AED 462M.' Never open with context and never let the explanation exceed four sentences before the number.

interview_soft.q: How do you give feedback to someone more senior than you?
interview_soft.a: Ask permission, be specific, and stay on observable behaviour and its effect. 'Can I give you a reaction to how the numbers landed in that meeting? When the forecast changed without the bridge, the room stopped trusting the rest of the pack.' No adjectives about them, one concrete instance, and a suggestion. Then stop talking. Most people either avoid this entirely or overcorrect into confrontation.

interview_soft.q: How do you influence people who do not report to you?
interview_soft.a: Retail finance is almost entirely this — Buying, Operations and Retail Heads do not report to you. The answer is currency: work out what each function is measured on and frame your ask in their terms. A buyer cares about sell-through and margin, not about your working capital target — so bring them the SKU-level analysis showing which lines tie up cash without turning. Give people the analysis they cannot build themselves, and influence follows. Name a specific instance and the outcome.
